title: Prophecy and discernment
hook: a word for someone, tested by scripture and the church (1 Corinthians 14:29)

segments.voice: Yesterday, laying on of hands: a hand on a shoulder and a prayer said over someone. Your line was a hand and a prayer. Whose shoulder came to mind? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

What should a church do when someone stands up and says God has given them a word? Paul faced that question in a letter. In the meetings he's writing to, one person has a psalm, another a teaching, another a word they say came from God, and they need an order to speak in. He doesn't tell them to stop. He gives them an order of service: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." Speak, then weigh. In Pentecostal and charismatic churches today, that pairing is still alive. Someone may stand during worship and say they sense a word for the room, or quietly tell one person something they believe God put on their heart. Then the church listens, and tests it. Today: prophecy and discernment.

In Paul's letter, prophecy isn't fortune-telling. He says what it's for in the same chapter: "he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." Edification means building up, and in the same letter Paul tells the church, "ye are God's building." Build up, urge on, comfort. Those are the three jobs. By Paul's measure, a word that only tears someone down has missed its job before anyone checks it. Then comes the weighing. Paul tells another church: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Both halves matter. Don't sneer at it, and don't swallow it whole. John's first letter says the same thing more sharply: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." In charismatic churches, a word is weighed against scripture by leaders and by the congregation, and the person who gave it is expected to take it humbly if it's set aside. A word doesn't outrank the Bible or the body. Christians read this gift in different ways, and it's worth saying who says what. Pentecostals and charismatics hold that the gift is still given today, as in the New Testament. Some other Protestants hold that prophecy as new revelation ended with the apostles, and hear Paul's words as being about preaching and teaching scripture. Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of prophetic gifts in the church, tested by the church's teaching. Here's the part that reaches an ordinary Tuesday. Words get spoken over people all the time: at work, at the dinner table, in a text at midnight. Paul's test works on any sentence. Does it build up?

Here's the practice: find a kind word for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind who could use building up this week. Let the words come slowly. Not flattery, and not advice. Something true about them that would hold weight, like a beam in a house. Then test it the way Paul asks. Does it build up, urge on, or comfort? If it does none of those, set it down and look for another. If you pray, you can hold that person before God while you choose. The bell holds the time.
Prophecy and discernment. A word spoken to build others up, and the church's work of weighing it against scripture.
Your line: build up. Today, give that person the kind word you found, plain and specific, and check that it does one of Paul's three jobs. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, someone may share a word they believe is from God, during worship or privately, and pastors and the congregation weigh it against scripture before anyone acts on it.

fork.setup: during worship someone stands and says God has given them a word. by Paul's instruction, what should the church do?
options: accept it at once, since it's from God.
let them speak, then weigh what was said.
silence them, since prophecy causes trouble.
fork.reveal: Paul does both: let the prophets speak, and let the others judge. the word is welcomed and tested.

original.note: Greek: a building, and the act of building up. Paul's word for what prophecy is for in 1 Corinthians 14:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: prophecy means predicting the future.
what it means: in Paul's letter, a word that builds up, urges on and comforts, and is weighed by others.
what a scholar hears: edification is a builder's word. in the same letter Paul tells the church, "ye are God's building."

notes: Hook paraphrases 1 Corinthians 14:26 (psalm, doctrine, revelation) and 14:27–31 (speaking in turn); 'people are talking over each other' is an inference from Paul's instructions; confirm it is fair.

'Edification is an old word for building up' and the original-game gloss of οἰκοδομή (building; building up) are lexical claims; confirm. 1 Corinthians 3:9 uses οἰκοδομή for 'building'; confirm before keeping the trapdoor's third floor.

Three positions summarized without ranking: continuationist (Pentecostal/charismatic), cessationist (some Protestants: prophecy as new revelation ended with the apostles; Paul's words applied to preaching), and Catholic/Orthodox (prophetic charisms tested by the church, e.g. Lumen Gentium 12). Confirm each is fairly put.
Description of charismatic practice (a word weighed by leaders and congregation against scripture; the speaker expected to accept correction) is general; confirm.
